svg.title: Active surveillance: getting in, getting out, and why people actually leave
svg.desc: A schematic that breaks active surveillance for low-risk papillary microcarcinoma into seven parts, to show that it is a set of written conditions rather than "let us watch and see". The first part is inclusion, in three cards side by side. American Thyroid Association 2025, recommendation 11A: the option is restricted to cT1aN0M0 papillary carcinoma - tumour 1 cm or smaller, no clinically suspicious neck nodes, no distant metastasis - as a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence, which in plain words means it may be done but the research holding it up is not of high quality. Korean Thyroid Association 2025, four conditions that must all hold at once: a fine-needle report of Bethesda category V or VI and 1 cm or smaller; no clinical nodal or distant metastasis; no obvious invasion of the strap muscles, trachea or recurrent laryngeal nerve on imaging; and none of the aggressive subtypes - tall cell, columnar cell, hobnail, solid or diffuse sclerosing. The same document recommends surgery for everyone under 19. The Japan Association of Endocrine Surgery consensus of 2021 lists seven further situations that go straight to surgery, of which the figure names two: the tumour sitting against the trachea and possibly already invading it, and the tumour lying on the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. That document states that evidence grading does not apply to it, so it carries no grade; and position sometimes matters more than size, since among papillary microcarcinomas smaller than 7 mm not one invaded the trachea or the recurrent laryngeal nerve at surgery. Next come the data above 1 cm: a single Japanese centre with a T1b cohort of only 61 people who chose surveillance; one American academic centre that widened the ceiling to 2 cm with 112 people under surveillance and a mean follow-up of 37.1 months; and the New York cohort of 291 people with intrathyroidal tumours up to 1.5 cm. Below them a crossed-out box reads "1.5 cm or 2 cm can be watched too": a few centres, a few people, short follow-up, and the ceiling that holds is 1 cm. This part closes with a gold panel stating that active surveillance is not something that has been proved but something that is permitted: the commissioned systematic review gathered seven studies comparing active surveillance with immediate surgery and seven further uncontrolled treatment series, only one study being rated "fair" and all the rest "poor", the source not saying whether that rating covers only the seven comparative studies or all fourteen, with the conclusion that methodological limitations prevent any strong conclusion; and while the 2021 Korean imaging consensus advises against biopsy first for certain highly suspicious nodules under 1 cm, being allowed to skip the needle is not the same as being allowed to decide alone. The second part is what is looked at during surveillance: neck ultrasound every 6 months for the first 1 to 2 years, then yearly if there is no progression, the same interval in all three documents. Beside it a second crossed-out box reads "measuring thyroglobulin during surveillance": recommendation 13 of the 2025 edition states that thyroglobulin is not measured during surveillance, nor are its antibodies, listed as good practice which the guideline does not grade, because the thyroid is still there intact and the number has no baseline against which to be read. The third part is the exit conditions, in two cards. The tumour side: growth of the primary by 3 mm or more; new biopsy-proven nodal metastasis; distant metastasis; extrathyroidal extension; and posterior growth, because behind the thyroid sit the trachea and the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The person side, written into the same recommendation rather than as a footnote: patient anxiety, inability to attend follow-up, and the patient saying they want surgery. A note records that the fourth Korean exit condition is simply that the patient chooses surgery, at the highest strength of recommendation; that growth must be present on two consecutive examinations at least 6 months apart; and that the Japanese size threshold is 13 mm. The fourth part is the probability of progression, in two cards. On the left, bars of the lifetime probability from the original Kuma paper (1,211 patients aged 20 to 79, estimated on surveillance to age 85): 60.3% in their twenties, 37.1% in their thirties, 27.3% in their forties, 14.9% in their fifties, 9.9% in their sixties and 3.5% in their seventies, with a note that the Japanese consensus transcribing the same paper lists a different and lower set that does not reconcile, and that what is drawn is the original abstract. On the right, ten-year progression by age in 1,235 Japanese patients: 22.5% under 40, 4.9% at 40 to 59 and 2.5% at 60 and over, with a note that progression there means growth to 12 mm or more or new nodal metastasis, not death. Three further cohorts are listed: Kuma Hospital over 30 years with 3,222 patients (growth of 3 mm or more in 3.8%, 4.7% at ten years, 6.6% at twenty; new nodal metastasis 0.8%, 1.0% at ten years, 1.6% at twenty; no thyroid cancer deaths); a Korean prospective cohort of 706 (composite progression 5.3% at two years and 14.2% at five, odds ratio 2.86 with 95% confidence interval 1.10 to 7.45 for those under 30); and the New York cohort of 291 (3.8% grew by 3 mm or more, cumulative 12.1% at five years, no regional or distant metastasis). The fifth part is who leaves. It quotes the 2025 guidelines - driven more by patient choice than signs of progression - and explains that the proportion going on to surgery varies between centres. A bar divided into five segments then shows the Japanese data on 2,288 people, of whom 162 (7.1%) converted to surgery after 12 months: disease progression 57, patient preference 43, physician preference 31, other thyroid or parathyroid disease 24, and other 7. Beside it, a Korean multicentre cohort of 370 in which 58 (15.7%) had delayed surgery, the commonest reason being anxiety at 37.9%, then tumour growth at 32.8% and nodal metastasis at 8.6%. A closing line says this is not failure: anxiety severe enough to affect daily life is written into the exit conditions, and holding out against surgery is not the goal. The sixth part is the price of operating later, drawn as intervals on a logarithmic axis with a dashed line marked "1 = no difference": delayed surgery gives transient hypoparathyroidism an odds ratio of 1.705 (95% confidence interval 1.188 to 2.448) and transient vocal cord palsy 1.519 (1.038 to 2.222), both intervals lying to the right of 1, while permanent hypoparathyroidism, permanent vocal cord palsy and recurrence all have intervals crossing 1 with no difference visible. The same part cites a 2025 meta-analysis of 21 studies and 9,397 people: disease progression during surveillance 14.53% (95% confidence interval 9.59 to 21.43) with no thyroid cancer deaths in either group, but with overall complications and recurrence both higher in the delayed-surgery group and a conclusion that active surveillance should be undertaken with caution. The seventh part is that the place doing this has conditions too. Ideal: an experienced multidisciplinary team, high-quality neck ultrasound, prospective data collection and a follow-up reminder system. Not suitable: reliable neck ultrasound unavailable or little experience of thyroid cancer, and on the patient side anyone unlikely to attend follow-up. The Japanese consensus requires a multidisciplinary team including an imaging specialist experienced in neck ultrasound as a necessary condition. The Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology requires a high-quality neck ultrasound by a specialist before starting, with "ideal / acceptable / not suitable" written into the report. The 2025 American guideline is the most direct: if the follow-up is not actually carried out, the safety claim for this approach does not hold. A panel beneath adds that there is no end point - all three guidelines say they do not know how long surveillance should run or at what age it may stop, the Japanese document concluding with lifelong surveillance and the American one writing that the necessary duration of follow-up remains unknown. The figure ends with a red-framed panel of readings that are barred: it does not say "let us watch and see"; it does not say "this is what the Japanese do"; it does not say watching is safer; it does not say the tumour hardly ever grows, since ten-year progression under 40 is 22.5% and the lifetime probability in their twenties is 60.3%; and holding out against surgery is not the goal. How much gland comes out is covered in "Half the gland, or all of it", how the nodule itself is sorted in "A scan found a nodule. Now what?", and how thyroglobulin is read in "Follow-up is an ultrasound and one number". At the foot are five questions to read out before taking this road: is mine cT1a and is it against the trachea or growing backwards; if I go into surveillance, how many months until the first ultrasound, who performs it, and do you have a follow-up reminder system; at how many millimetres would you tell me to have surgery; at my age, which cell does my lifetime probability of progression fall in; and if I start losing sleep over this, may I say at any point that I want surgery.

g.text: ACTIVE SURVEILLANCE - THE CONDITIONS, THE EXITS, AND WHO ACTUALLY LEAVES
Active surveillance is a set of written conditions, not "let
us watch and see"
Inclusion conditions, exit conditions, an imaging interval and requirements on the team: all four are written down. If any one of
them does not hold, this road does not hold.
And the people who actually leave surveillance mostly leave for reasons that are not the tumour. This figure draws that
proportion.
One - getting in: the ceiling is still 1 cm
American Thyroid Association 2025, recommendation 11A, restricted to cT1aN0M0 papillary carcinoma; a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence.
American Thyroid Association 2025
cT1aN0M0 papillary carcinoma: an
option that may be offered
Tumour 1 cm or smaller.
No clinically suspicious neck nodes.
No distant metastasis.
Conditional recommendation, low-certainty
evidence - in plain words: it may be done, but the
research holding it up is not of high quality.
Korean Thyroid Association 2025
Four conditions, all of which must hold
at once
A fine-needle report of Bethesda category V or
VI, 1 cm or smaller.
No clinical nodal or distant metastasis.
No obvious invasion of the strap muscles,
trachea or recurrent laryngeal nerve on
imaging.
Not one of the aggressive subtypes: tall cell,
columnar cell, hobnail, solid or diffuse
sclerosing.
The same document adds: surgery is
recommended for everyone under 19.
Japan Association of Endocrine Surgery 2021
Seven further situations that go
straight to surgery
The tumour sits against the trachea and may
already have invaded it.
The tumour lies on the course of the recurrent
laryngeal nerve.
That document states that evidence grading
does not apply to it, so it carries no grade.
Position sometimes matters more than size:
among papillary microcarcinomas smaller than 7
mm, not one invaded the trachea or the recurrent
laryngeal nerve at surgery.
Above 1 cm the data are thin
A single Japanese centre had a T1b cohort of only 61 people who chose surveillance.
One American academic centre widened the ceiling to 2 cm: 112 people under surveillance, mean follow-up 37.1 months.
The New York cohort took intrathyroidal tumours up to 1.5 cm: 291 people.
"1.5 cm or 2 cm can be watched too"
A few centres, a few people, short follow-up. The ceiling that holds is 1 cm,
and this figure does not draw it any wider.
Active surveillance is not something that has been proved; it is something that is permitted
The systematic review commissioned for this edition gathered seven studies comparing active surveillance with immediate surgery, and seven further uncontrolled
treatment series. Only one study was rated "fair" in quality and all the rest were rated "poor" (the source does not say whether that rating covers only the seven
comparative studies or all fourteen); the conclusion was that methodological limitations prevent any strong conclusion.
The 2021 Korean imaging consensus advises against biopsy first for certain highly suspicious nodules under 1 cm. "You may skip the needle" is not the same as "you may
decide this yourself": every condition below still has to hold.
Two - what is looked at during surveillance, and what is not
Neck ultrasound every 6 months for the first 1 to 2 years, then yearly if there is no progression
All three documents give the same interval: the American Thyroid Association 2025 guidelines, the Korean Thyroid Association 2025 guideline and the 2021 Japanese
consensus.
Measuring thyroglobulin during surveillance
Recommendation 13 of the 2025 edition: thyroglobulin is not measured during
surveillance, nor are its antibodies. It is listed as good practice, which the
guideline does not grade. The reason is simple - the thyroid is still there
intact, so the number has no baseline against which to be read. How it is
read is in "Follow-up is an ultrasound and one number".
Three - getting out: what stops surveillance and sends you to surgery
Recommendation 14 of the 2025 edition lists the exit conditions in one string, also as good practice, which the guideline does not grade.
The tumour side
The primary tumour grows by 3 mm or more.
New, biopsy-proven nodal metastasis.
Distant metastasis.
Extrathyroidal extension appears.
The tumour grows posteriorly - because behind the thyroid sit the trachea
and the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The person side (written into the same recommendation, not a
footnote)
Patient anxiety.
Inability to attend follow-up reliably.
The patient says they want surgery.
The fourth Korean exit condition is simply "the patient chooses to have surgery", at the highest strength of recommendation. The same document requires that growth be present on two
consecutive examinations at least 6 months apart, because ultrasound measurement carries error of its own. The Japanese size threshold is 13 mm.
Four - the probability of progression, cell by age
"It hardly ever grows" does not hold for young people.
Lifetime probability of progression (the original Kuma paper: 1,211 patients
aged 20 to 79, estimated on surveillance to age 85)
In their twenties
In their thirties
In their forties
In their fifties
In their sixties
In their
seventies
The Japanese consensus, transcribing the same paper, lists a different and
lower set of numbers; the two do not reconcile. What is drawn here is the set in
the original abstract.
Ten-year progression by age (1,235 people, Japan)
Under 40
60 and over
"Progression" in that set means growth to 12 mm or more, or new nodal
metastasis. It does not mean death.
Kuma Hospital, 30 years, 3,222 low-risk papillary microcarcinomas under surveillance:
growth of 3 mm or more in 3.8%, 4.7% at ten years and 6.6% at twenty; new nodal
metastasis in 0.8%, 1.0% at ten years and 1.6% at twenty; and not one death from thyroid
cancer.
A Korean prospective cohort of 706 people: composite progression 5.3% at two years and
14.2% at five; for those under 30 the odds ratio was 2.86 (95% confidence interval 1.10 to
7.45) - an odds ratio is the chance of something happening in one group divided by the
chance in another, and this interval does not cross 1.
The New York cohort of 291: 3.8% grew by 3 mm or more, a cumulative 12.1% at five
years, and no regional or distant metastasis.
Five - the real reasons people leave are mostly not the tumour
“driven more by patient choice than signs of progression”
American Thyroid Association 2025 guidelines: the proportion who go on to surgery varies between centres, and is driven more by patient choice than by signs of
progression.
Japanese data on 2,288 people: 162 (7.1%) converted to surgery after 12 months
Disease progression, 57
Patient preference, 43
Physician preference, 31
Other thyroid or parathyroid disease, 24
Other, 7
In a Korean multicentre cohort of 370 people, 58 (15.7%) had delayed surgery. The commonest reason was anxiety, at 37.9%; tumour growth accounted for 32.8% and nodal
metastasis for 8.6%.
This is not failure. Anxiety severe enough to affect daily life is written into the exit conditions. Holding out against surgery is not the goal of this road.
Six - operating later has a price, and it lands in the "transient" cell
Delayed surgery: transient hypoparathyroidism
Odds ratio 1.705 (95% confidence interval 1.188 to 2.448)
Delayed surgery: transient vocal cord palsy
Odds ratio 1.519 (95% confidence interval 1.038 to 2.222)
1 = no difference
A meta-analysis of six studies by the Korean Thyroid Association itself. For permanent hypoparathyroidism, permanent vocal cord palsy and recurrence, all three
intervals cross 1 and no difference can be seen.
A 2025 meta-analysis of 21 studies and 9,397 people: disease progression during surveillance 14.53% (95% confidence interval 9.59 to 21.43), with no thyroid cancer
deaths in either group; but its conclusion was that overall complications and recurrence were both higher in the delayed-surgery group, and it wrote that active
surveillance should be undertaken with caution.
Seven - the place doing this has conditions attached as well
Ideal
An experienced multidisciplinary team, high-quality neck ultrasound, prospective data collection and a follow-up
reminder system.
Not suitable
Reliable neck ultrasound is not available, or there is little experience of managing thyroid cancer; on the patient side,
someone unlikely to attend follow-up is also listed as not suitable.
The Japanese consensus puts it more strongly
A multidisciplinary team including an imaging specialist experienced in neck ultrasound is a necessary condition.
Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology
A high-quality neck ultrasound by a specialist before starting, with "ideal / acceptable / not suitable" written into the
report.
The 2025 American guideline is the most direct
If the follow-up is not actually carried out, the safety claim for this approach does not hold.
And there is no end point
All three guidelines say they do not know how long surveillance should run, or at what age it may stop. The Japanese document concludes with lifelong surveillance; the
American one writes that the necessary duration of follow-up remains unknown.
What is being accepted is not only the absence of an operation, but a schedule with no end.
What this figure must not be read to say
It does not say "let us watch and see". The inclusion conditions, the exit conditions, the imaging interval and the team all have to hold; "I have decided
not to be operated on for now" does not exist in the text - it takes your willingness and a team that can actually do it.
It does not say "this is what the Japanese do". Recommendation 11A of the 2025 edition is conditional with low-certainty evidence, and in the
commissioned systematic review only one study was rated "fair" and all the rest "poor" - the source not saying whether that rating covers only the
seven comparative studies or all fourteen.
It does not say watching is safer. Nothing increases in the permanent cell, but transient hypoparathyroidism at 1.705 and transient vocal cord palsy at
1.519 are both above 1, and a meta-analysis of 9,397 people found recurrence higher too.
It does not say "it hardly ever grows". Ten-year progression under 40 is 22.5%, and the lifetime probability for someone in their twenties is 60.3%.
And holding out against surgery is not the goal: anxiety, inability to attend follow-up and the patient asking for an operation are all written into the exit
conditions. How much gland comes out is in "Half the gland, or all of it"; how the nodule itself is sorted is in "A scan found a nodule. Now what?".
Five things to ask before taking this road
Is mine cT1a? Is it against the trachea, or growing backwards?
If I go into surveillance, how many months until the first ultrasound? Who performs it? Do you have a follow-up reminder system?
At how many millimetres would you tell me to have surgery?
At my age, which cell does my lifetime probability of progression fall in?
If I start losing sleep over this, may I say at any point that I want surgery?
Schematic, redrawn from the 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines for differentiated thyroid cancer, the 2025 Korean Thyroid Association active
surveillance guideline, the 2024 Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology consensus, the 2021 Japan Association of Endocrine Surgery consensus and the Kuma
Hospital, New York and Korean multicentre cohorts; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying
studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
